name: Wei Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mondays and Wednesdays I've got lectures from nine, then a seminar about how cities get planned. I live in a shared house with two other lads, forty minutes away on the bus. Saturdays and Sundays I stack shelves at a supermarket depot, and that pays for my food and my bus pass. The reading piles up faster than I can do it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What has surprised you most so far?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: How alone you can feel in a lecture hall of two hundred people. At school the teachers knew my name. Here I'm a number on a list, and I'm already behind on my first essay because the depot shifts ate the weekend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. That one is called AI Plateau. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it's mostly hype, like plenty of things before it. My housemates go on about AI all the time and I just shrug. If it only saves people five minutes on emails, fine, that's not my problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm still scared, just not of AI. My loan is already huge and the depot cut my shifts twice this year, so a quiet AI world still isn't a calm one for me. A sociology degree feels like a bet I could lose whatever the computers do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. I'll keep my two shifts, hand in essays on time and stay away from the AI tools. If the depot supervisor offers a Friday evening I'll take it, because every extra week of rent money counts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat, honestly. I'm relieved nothing is exploding, but nothing gets easier either. The money pressure just sits there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the depot cut your shifts twice. What happened the last time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They dropped me from three shifts to two in September, no warning, just a new rota on the noticeboard. I skipped renewing my bus pass for a month and walked the long way. My mum covered my phone bill and told me not to tell anyone, which made me feel worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you stay away from AI tools, even for study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I think it's lazy and the university can tell. I also like working things out myself, even when it's slow. My seminar tutor said the whole point is to think, and I took that seriously, maybe too seriously.

say: I'd say AI is **mostly hype** and I won't lose sleep over it.
I'd tell friends the real problem is the cost of **rent and food**, not computers.
think: I'm scared of my **loan** and my shifts being cut, whatever AI does.
I worry a sociology degree won't be worth the **debt** I'm taking on.
do: Keep both **weekend shifts** at the depot and ask for a Friday evening.
Hand in every essay on time and keep doing the reading **myself**.
feel: Flat and a little relieved, but the **money worry** never goes away.
S0.quote: My loan is already huge and the depot cut my shifts twice this year, so a quiet AI world still isn't a calm one for me.
fieldNote: Wei talks about AI as someone else's topic; his fear is entirely about **money**.
Says nothing changes, yet his answers are full of rent and shift cuts.
Mentions his mum paying his phone bill with real embarrassment.

steps.text: Keep both weekend shifts at the supermarket depot
Ask the supervisor for a Friday evening shift

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. That one is called Steady Disruption. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to hit people who sit at desks, and the bosses will call it progress while they cut the junior jobs. Somebody has to speak up for people at the bottom. I'd say that in my seminar and I'd say it to my housemates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the jobs I'm heading for are exactly the ones that shrink: office admin, research assistant, council paperwork. A business or social science graduate does a lot of writing and checking, which is the stuff AI takes first. My plan B is thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the students' union and the campaign about graduate jobs, because I don't trust anyone to look after us otherwise. I'd also try to get a placement or volunteer with a housing charity in the second year, so I have something real on my CV. I still wouldn't use AI to write essays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry, more than scared. It feels like the people who already have money get the benefits and people like me get told to adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't use AI. Wouldn't that put you behind others in your year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. A girl on my course uses it for every summary and she gets her work done in half the time. But if everyone has the same tool, what makes me employable? I'd rather be the one who can argue a point face to face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if graduate jobs shrink?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big firms first, because they'll save money and call it innovation. Then the government, for letting them do it without any rules. I don't blame the students who use the tools, they're just trying to survive.

say: I'd say bosses will call it progress while they **cut junior jobs**.
I'd say we need **rules** and a stronger students' union.
think: My own jobs, **admin and research**, are exactly what AI takes first.
I have a thin **plan B**, and I know it.
do: Join the **students' union** campaign on graduate jobs this term.
Volunteer with a **housing charity** in second year for real experience.
feel: **Angry** more than scared, because the rewards go to people who already have money.
S1.quote: A business or social science graduate does a lot of writing and checking, which is the stuff AI takes first.
fieldNote: Turns worry into **anger at firms** and the government rather than personal fear.
Refuses AI on principle even after seeing a course-mate benefit.
Sees collective action as the only protection he trusts.

steps.text: Join the students' union graduate jobs campaign
Write to my local MP about rules on AI hiring
Volunteer with the housing charity in second year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. That one is called AGI by 2028. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disaster and nobody is ready, not the university, not the government and certainly not my mum. Two years is nothing. I'd be online asking why nobody voted on this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think my degree is done for before I even finish it. I graduate around 2029, and the card says thinking work goes in 2028. Then the robots come in 2031 and my depot job goes too, so I lose both the career and the weekend job. I can't see where I'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably drop out of the idea of a career and try to get a full-time job at the depot, or something hands-on, while that still exists. I'd ask my mum to look at an apprenticeship with me. I'd also go to every union meeting going, because that's the only thing that gives me any power.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, properly. My stomach would go every time I opened the news. I'd be on the loan paperwork thinking I'm paying for a thing that doesn't exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years, what changes compared to having longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's no time to retrain or even finish a normal degree. With a longer gap I could build a plan. With two years I'm just reacting, and I'm someone who hates being rushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you tell first, and what would you say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum. I'd say I'm sorry, I can't keep up the plan we made, and I need us to think again. She cleans offices at night and she'd say don't worry, which would make it worse.

say: I'd say **nobody is ready** and that this was done without a vote.
I'd go to every **union meeting** I could.
think: My degree could be **worthless** before I even graduate in 2029.
Robots would take my **depot job** too, so I'd lose both.
do: Look for **full-time depot** or hands-on work while it still exists.
Ask my mum to look at an **apprenticeship** with me.
feel: **Sick**, with my stomach turning each time I read the news.
S2.quote: I'd be on the loan paperwork thinking I'm paying for a thing that doesn't exist.
fieldNote: First scenario where he sees **both** his degree and his weekend job disappearing.
Hates being rushed; his resistant side makes short warning hit hardest.
Protective of his mum and worries about disappointing her.

steps.text: Apply for full-time depot work and other hands-on jobs
Look at apprenticeships with my mum
Go to every union meeting near the university
Talk through the loan and my plans with my mum

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. That one is called AGI by 2031. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a bit more breathing room but it's still too fast, and people need a plan now. I'd tell my housemates to stop treating it as a joke. If anything, I'd push for the university to change what it teaches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think I might just about get a degree in before it lands, but I'd come out in 2029 with two years of notice and a big loan. That's better than 2028, but not by much. I'd feel like I'm walking toward a door that's closing slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, because dropping out with the debt is worse, and try to pick modules that involve talking to people, like community work. I'd keep the depot job and save something each month, even twenty a week. I'd also try to build links with a union, because a graduate with no contacts is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can handle that. There's time for a plan, and I like having a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change in the first year, while you can see it coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop leaving everything to the last minute. I'd go to the careers office, which I've skipped, and ask what the plan is for people like me. I'd also start saving, even small, in a separate account my mum can't dip into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would five years compare to the two-year version for your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd have time to adjust, and maybe cut her night shifts back if I'm earning. In the two-year one she'd be panicking with me. Here I could at least show her a spreadsheet.

say: I'd say five years is **still too fast** and we need a plan now.
I'd push the university to teach **people-facing** skills.
think: I'd get my degree but leave in 2029 with a **big loan** and little notice.
It feels like walking towards a **closing door**.
do: Finish the degree and pick **community-work modules** with real people contact.
Save **twenty a week** from the depot in a separate account.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to cope because there's time for a plan.
S3.quote: I'd feel like I'm walking toward a door that's closing slowly.
fieldNote: The extra time makes him **practical**, with a savings and careers-office plan.
Still carries the loan as the main source of fear.
Wants to show his mum a spreadsheet, a sign of how he reassures her.

steps.text: Save twenty a week in a separate account
Book a careers office appointment this term
Keep the weekend depot shifts through second year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. That one is called AGI by 2036. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to sort things out if people act early, so let's actually do it. Governments need to bring in rules, training and some kind of support before it lands. I'd say the same to anyone who thinks it's far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd be fine, kind of. By 2036 I'd be twenty-eight, with a job and some savings, if I'd used the time well. But I'm resistant to change and I know I'd put it off, so it worries me that I'd waste the decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, get a job in housing or policy for a few years, and pay down the loan hard. I'd start learning basic AI tools in the second half, probably around 2030, because by then it wouldn't feel like cheating. I'd keep one foot in hands-on work, maybe a trade course in the evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A decade is long enough that I could stop being afraid and start being practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might put it off. What would stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A deadline from someone else. If a union or my tutor said, here's the course you do by next spring, I'd do it. Left alone I'd keep saying next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we have time, and that she doesn't have to worry about my loan on her night shifts. I'd say, I'll work it out in my own way, and I mean it this time.

say: I'd say ten years is **enough time** if people act early.
I'd say governments must bring in **rules and training** soon.
think: By 2036 I'd be **twenty-eight** and probably fine, if I use the time well.
I know I **put things off**, and that frightens me.
do: Finish the degree and take a **housing or policy job** to pay the loan.
Learn **basic AI tools** around 2030 and take an evening trade course.
feel: Mostly **okay**, because a decade lets me be practical instead of afraid.
S4.quote: A decade is long enough that I could stop being afraid and start being practical.
fieldNote: Only scenario where Wei **relaxes**, and mostly because of time.
Honest about procrastination; needs outside deadlines.
Finally imagines using AI tools, but only years from now.

steps.text: Finish the degree and aim for a housing or policy job
Pay the student loan down hard in the first years
Join a union campaign for training rights

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. It's too fast, it puts my degree and my weekend job under threat at the same time, and I'd be reacting instead of planning. What would help is a real plan from the government and the union, some rules for firms, and someone telling students straight what jobs are likely to exist.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people assume students are fine because we have loans and time. I'm already skipping a bus pass some months. If there's one thing to take from this, it's that worry about money was there long before AI.

headlineQuote: Worry about money was there long before AI.
portrait: Wei, 18, studies **sociology and politics** and lives in a shared house, working weekends at a supermarket depot.
He never uses AI, calls it lazy, and blames **big firms** and weak government for what comes.
His thin money and loan make even quiet scenarios feel **anxious**.
The two-year warning scares him most; ten years lets him relax a bit.
He turns worry into union action and wants to protect his mum, who cleans offices at night.
biggestWorry: The **two-year AGI** picture worries him most, because it threatens his degree and weekend job at once.
whatWouldHelp: A **real plan** from government and unions, rules for firms, and honest advice on likely jobs.
